entry: Japanese anime television series produced by Toei Animation. It is a direct sequel to the 1986 [[Dragon Ball]] series and adapts the remaining 325 chapters of the manga by [[Akira Toriyama]]. It aired on Fuji Television from April 1989 to January 1996 and was dubbed in at least 81 countries. Its success spawned films, video games and merchandise, and the series remains a cultural icon.

Japanese role-playing video game franchise. Created by Yuji Horii, with character designer [[Akira Toriyama]] and composer Koichi Sugiyama, its first game was published in 1986, and it has eleven main-series games. It was published as Dragon Warrior in North America until 2005 to avoid a trademark conflict. Its games feature turn-based combat and recurring monsters, including the Slime, which became the series' mascot, and the franchise has spawned [[Manga|manga]], [[Anime|anime]] and novels.

Fruit of several [[Cactus|cactus]] species in the genus Selenicereus, also called pitahaya or pitaya. The most common species, *Selenicereus undatus*, is native to southern Mexico and the Pacific coast of Guatemala, Costa Rica and El Salvador. By the turn of the 21st century its cultivation had expanded to China, [[Colombia]] and most of [[Southeast Asia]]. Its flowers open only at night, and bats are a natural pollinator.

Flying insect of the suborder Anisoptera in the order [[Odonata]]. About 3,000 living species are known, most of them tropical. Adults have a pair of large, multifaceted [[Compound eye|compound eyes]], two pairs of strong transparent wings and an elongated body, and many have iridescent or metallic colors. Dragonflies are [[Predation|predatory]] both as aquatic nymphs and as adults, and they are fast, agile fliers capable of accurate aerial ambush. Nymphs can live up to five years, while most adults survive about five weeks or less. Unlike [[Damselfly|damselflies]], which fold their wings at rest, dragonflies hold their wings flat and away from the body. True dragonflies first appeared in the Early Jurassic, while their larger relatives, the Meganisoptera, lived in the [[Carboniferous]]. Loss of [[Wetland|wetland]] habitat threatens dragonfly populations worldwide.

Natural or artificial removal of surface and subsurface water from land with excess water. Internal drainage can prevent severe waterlogging in most agricultural [[Soil|soils]], but many soils need artificial drainage to improve production or manage water supplies. The Indus Valley Civilization had sewerage and drainage systems, and houses in [[Mohenjo-daro]] had drainage facilities. New storm water systems incorporate geotextile filters that keep fine soil from clogging the drain. Monitoring by [[Seattle]] Public Utilities reported a 99 percent reduction in storm water leaving a pilot street project designed to mimic natural drainage. In the UK, local planning has been required by law since 2010 to factor sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS) into development.

Land area in which all flowing surface water converges to a single point or body of water. It is bounded by the drainage divide, a perimeter of ridges and hills that separates adjacent basins. Smaller basins may merge at river confluences, forming a hierarchical pattern. In North America a drainage basin is commonly called a watershed. In an endorheic basin, water converges on an interior sink, such as a permanent lake, a dry lake or a point where surface water is lost underground. About 48.71% of the world's land drains into the [[Atlantic Ocean]], and just over 13% into the [[Pacific Ocean]]. The five largest river basins by area are those of the Amazon (7 million sq km), the Congo (4 million sq km), the Nile (3.4 million sq km), the Mississippi (3.22 million sq km) and the [[Río de la Plata]] (3.17 million sq km).

Body of water between [[Cape Horn]] in [[Chile]] and the South Shetland Islands of [[Antarctica]]. It connects the southwestern Atlantic (Scotia Sea) with the southeastern Pacific and is the narrowest passage around Antarctica, so it strongly influences Antarctic and global ocean circulation and climate. Named after the 16th-century English explorer and privateer [[Francis Drake|Sir Francis Drake]], it is considered one of the most treacherous crossings for ships, since the Antarctic Circumpolar Current meets no resistance from any landmass and waves top 40 feet (12 m). The Dutch navigator Willem Schouten was the first to sail through it, in 1616. In 2019 a crew of six became the first to row across it. The passage opened as Antarctica separated from [[South America]] through [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]], though estimates of when range from 49 to 17 million years ago.

Probabilistic formula estimating the number of active, communicative extraterrestrial civilizations in the [[Milky Way]]. Frank Drake formulated it in 1961 as a way to stimulate scientific dialogue at the first meeting on the [[Search for extraterrestrial intelligence|search for extraterrestrial intelligence]] (SETI). It is more an approximation than a precise count, and its factors, such as the fraction of stars with planets and the average number of life-supporting planets per star, are highly conjectural. The resulting uncertainty is so large that the equation cannot draw firm conclusions.

Canadian rapper, singer and actor. He first gained recognition as Jimmy Brooks in the television series *Degrassi: The Next Generation*. His debut album, *Thank Me Later* (2010), topped the Billboard 200, and *Views* (2016) led the Billboard 200 for 13 weeks. He founded the record label OVO Sound and has won 5 [[Grammy Awards]]. With over 170 million units sold, he is among the world's best-selling music artists. He has publicly feuded with [[Kanye West]] and [[Kendrick Lamar]].

Mountain range forming the eastern part of the Great Escarpment in southern Africa. The escarpment stretches more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) from the Eastern Cape Province northward, forming much of the border between [[Lesotho]] and [[KwaZulu-Natal]]. The Great Escarpment's greatest elevation, 2,000 to 3,482 m (6,562 to 11,424 ft), lies in the border region of [[South Africa]] and Lesotho. Its steep rift walls formed during the breakup of southern [[Gondwana]]. The Zulu name uKhahlamba and the Sotho name Maloti both mean barrier of up-pointed spears, while the Afrikaans name Drakensberge means Dragons' Mountains. The transboundary Maloti-Drakensberg Park is a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], and the uKhahlamba-Drakensberg contains the largest concentration of [[Rock art|rock art]] in Africa south of the Sahara.

Specific mode of fiction represented in performance, such as a play, opera, mime or ballet. Considered as a genre of poetry, the dramatic mode has been contrasted with the epic and lyric modes since [[Aristotle]]'s *Poetics* (c. 335 BC), the earliest work of dramatic theory. The word comes from a Greek term meaning deed or act, and its two masks represent the traditional division between comedy and tragedy. Western drama originated in classical Athens, which produced tragedy, comedy and the satyr play for competitions held in honor of [[Dionysus]] from the 5th century BC. The oldest surviving drama is [[Aeschylus]]' *The Persians*. In the modern era, drama came to mean a play that is neither comedy nor tragedy, and the term became a genre in film and television. Mime, in which the story is told through movement alone, and musicals, which combine speech and song, are also forms of drama.

Language family spoken by 250 million people, primarily in South India. The most widely spoken are Telugu, Tamil, [[Kannada]] and [[Malayalam]], all with long literary traditions. Smaller literary languages include Tulu and Kodava. Dravidian is first attested in the 2nd century BCE in Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions on cave walls in the [[Madurai]] and Tirunelveli districts of [[Tamil Nadu]]. In 1816 Francis Whyte Ellis argued that these languages descended from a common non-[[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]] ancestor. In 1856 Robert Caldwell coined the term Dravidian for the family. The family has not been shown to be related to any other.

Early 20th-century [[Battleship|battleship]] type. It takes its name from HMS Dreadnought, launched by the [[Royal Navy]] in 1906 with an all-big-gun armament and [[Steam turbine|steam turbine]] propulsion. Its launch renewed the naval arms race between the United Kingdom and Germany, and older battleships became known as pre-dreadnoughts. Most original dreadnoughts were scrapped after [[World War I]] under the Washington Naval Treaty. The only battle between large dreadnought fleets, at [[Battle of Jutland|Jutland]] in 1916, ended without a decisive result.

Vernacular Chinese novel by Cao Xueqin, also called *The Story of the Stone*. Considered one of the Four Great Classic Novels of [[Chinese literature]], it is known for its psychological scope and its portrayal of social relations in High Qing China. Its plot depicts the rise and decline of a family much like Cao's own, and the novel is intended as a memorial to the women he knew in his youth. Cao began writing it in the 1740s. Printed editions edited by Cheng Weiyuan and Gao E in 1791 to 1792 added 40 chapters, forming a 120-chapter version that became the most widely circulated. The novel is written in vernacular Chinese, and its dialogue is rendered in the Beijing Mandarin dialect.

Final home video game console manufactured by [[Sega]]. Released in Japan on November 27, 1998, and worldwide in late 1999, it was the first sixth-generation console and the first to include a built-in modem for online play. Sales declined as Sony built anticipation for the [[PlayStation 2]], and Sega discontinued the console on March 31, 2001, after 9.13 million units sold worldwide. Over 600 games were produced for it. Many of its games, including *Sonic Adventure* and *Shenmue*, are regarded as innovative.

Capital city of the German state of [[Saxony]] and its second most populous city after Leipzig. It lies on the [[Elbe]] River, and its urban area has over 780,000 inhabitants. First documented in 1206, it became the residence of the Wettin rulers and later the capital of the Electorate and Kingdom of Saxony, earning the nickname Jewel Box for its [[Baroque]] and [[Rococo]] center. American and British bombing near the end of [[World War II]] killed approximately 25,000 people, most of them civilians, and destroyed much of the center. After the war Dresden was part of [[East Germany]]. Since [[German reunification]] in 1990, extensive parts of the historic center have been rebuilt, including the Frauenkirche, which was rebuilt between 1994 and 2005.

One-piece outer garment worn on the torso, hanging down over the legs. Also called a frock or gown, a dress often consists of a bodice attached to a [[Skirt|skirt]]. Shapes, sleeve lengths, necklines and hemlines vary with [[Fashion|fashion]] trends, modesty, weather and personal taste, and dresses suit both formal and casual wear. Historically, structural garments such as corsets, petticoats, panniers and bustles were used to achieve the desired silhouette. In the 11th century European women wore loose garments similar in shape to men's tunics, and by the 15th century houppelandes and gowns were popular. From the 1540s bodices were stiffened and skirts shaped with a Spanish farthingale. Women's dresses in [[Russia]] during the 16th and 17th centuries identified the wearer's place in society or family.

Political scandal that divided the French Third Republic from 1894 until 1906. Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish artillery officer, was wrongly convicted of treason in December 1894 for passing military secrets to the German embassy in [[Paris]] and was sent to the penal colony on Devil's Island in [[French Guiana]]. In 1896 Lieutenant Colonel Georges Picquart identified Major Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy as the real culprit, but military officials suppressed the evidence and Esterhazy was acquitted. [[Émile Zola]]'s open letter "J'Accuse...!" stoked support for Dreyfus. He was retried and reconvicted in 1899, then pardoned, and was exonerated in 1906. The affair divided France between Dreyfusards, including [[Sarah Bernhardt]] and [[Georges Clemenceau]], and pro-army, mostly Catholic anti-Dreyfusards. It remains a notable example of a miscarriage of justice and of [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]].

Cutting process producing a hole of circular cross-section in solid materials. A usually multi-point rotary bit is pressed against the workpiece and turned at hundreds to thousands of revolutions per minute, cutting off chips. In [[Rock (geology)|rock]] drilling the hole is usually made by hammering the bit with quickly repeated short movements, either from outside the hole or within it. Drilling can leave a thin, highly stressed surface layer that makes the workpiece more susceptible to [[Corrosion|corrosion]] and crack propagation, so a finish operation may be used. Cutting fluid cools the bit, increases tool life and helps eject chips. Spot drilling creates a guide hole for the final drilling.

Ingestion of water or other liquids into the body, usually through the [[Mouth|mouth]]. Humans drink by swallowing, with peristalsis carrying the liquid through the [[Esophagus|esophagus]] to the [[Stomach|stomach]]. Most animals drink to maintain hydration, though many survive on water gained from their food. [[Cat|Cats]] lap with the tip of the tongue, ruminants draw in water by a plunging action, and [[Elephant|elephants]] draw water into their trunks and squirt it into their mouths. Most birds scoop water into their bills, while the common pigeon can suck it in directly. [[Amphibian|Amphibians]] and freshwater animals absorb water through their skin, while saltwater fish drink and purge excess salt through their gills. Lack of hydration causes thirst, which is regulated by the hypothalamus, and both inadequate and excessive water intake are linked to health problems.

Controlled operation and movement of a land vehicle, such as a [[Car|car]], [[Bus|bus]], [[Truck|truck]] or [[Taxi|taxi]]. In many countries drivers must pass practical and theoretical tests to obtain a license, and they must follow the road and traffic laws of their location. Driving requires physical skills, such as steering, gear shifting and braking, and mental skills, such as hazard awareness and decision-making. In 1888 Bertha Benz made the first long-distance automobile trip, driving from Mannheim to Pforzheim in [[Germany]]. Safety concerns include poor road conditions, speeding, [[Driving under the influence|impaired driving]] and texting. As of 2023, the [[World Health Organization]] estimated that 1.19 million people are killed annually in road traffic accidents, and that road injury is the leading cause of death for people aged 5 to 29.

Crime of driving or operating a vehicle while impaired by [[Alcohol (drug)|alcohol]] or other [[Drug|drugs]]. The offense is also called driving while intoxicated (DWI) or operating while intoxicated, and its name varies between jurisdictions. In most U.S. states it covers being in physical control of a motor vehicle, even when it is not moving. Many DUI laws also apply to motorcycling, boating, piloting aircraft, riding horses and cycling. The first person convicted of driving a motor vehicle while intoxicated was George Smith, a London [[Taxi|taxi]] driver, on September 10, 1897. A small increase in blood alcohol content raises the relative risk of a motor vehicle crash.

One-humped [[Camel|camel]] of the genus *Camelus*, the tallest of the three camel species. Adult males stand 1.8 to 2.4 m (5.9 to 7.9 ft) at the shoulder and weigh between 400 and 690 kg (880 and 1,520 lb). Its long curved neck, narrow chest and single hump distinguish it, and it can tolerate losing more than 30% of its total water content. The dromedary feeds on desert vegetation and forms herds of about 20 individuals, led by a dominant male. It has not occurred naturally in the wild for nearly 2,000 years and was probably first domesticated in the [[Arabian Peninsula]] about 4,000 years ago. Domesticated herds are kept in arid regions of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and the Thar Desert, and a feral population occurs in Australia. [[Carl Linnaeus]] gave it its binomial name in 1758.

Species of fly in the family Drosophilidae, widely used as a [[Model organism|model organism]] in biological research. Also called the fruit fly or vinegar fly, it is attracted to rotting fruit and fermenting beverages and is a common pest in homes and restaurants. Charles W. Woodworth first proposed its use as a model organism in 1901. Its rapid life cycle, relatively simple genetics with four pairs of [[Chromosome|chromosomes]] and large number of offspring make it useful in research on genetics, physiology and life history evolution. The species was originally African, and it now occurs on all continents, including islands. In 1947 it became the first animal launched into space. As of 2017, six [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prizes]] had been awarded to scientists working with it.

Period of drier-than-normal conditions, lasting days, months or years. Drought has large effects on [[Ecosystem|ecosystems]] and [[Agriculture|agriculture]] and harms local economies, disrupting food supply, livestock farming, [[Hydropower|hydropower]] and river navigation. Heat waves can worsen drought by increasing evapotranspiration, which dries out vegetation and increases fuel for [[Wildfire|wildfires]]. Drought is a recurring feature of climate, and [[Climate change|climate change]] is making it more extreme and less predictable. Regions at increased risk include the Amazon basin, [[Australia]], the [[Sahel]] and [[India]]; in 2005 parts of the Amazon basin experienced the worst drought in 100 years. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's Sixth Assessment Report defines drought simply as drier than normal conditions. Drought is commonly divided into meteorological, hydrological and agricultural types.
